title: Superscalar Issue Width: 4-way vs. 2-way
where_in_paper: Issue width and pipeline depth sections; likely in the microarchitecture overview or the instruction delivery pipeline discussion
decision: The 21264 was designed as a 4-way superscalar processor capable of issuing up to 4 instructions per clock cycle
alternatives_or_rejected: A 2-way or 3-way superscalar design would have been simpler to implement with lower hardware overhead and potentially faster clock speeds; an 8-way design was likely considered but rejected due to the exponential increase in issue logic complexity, register file ports, and scheduling complexity
rationale: The paper discusses that 4-way provides a good balance between the performance gains of wider issue (which provides diminishing returns beyond 4) and the hardware cost. The 4-way design required substantial register file ports (8 read + 4 write ports for the integer register file) and complex scheduling logic, but the performance gain over 2-3 way justified the cost. The paper notes that wider issue provides diminishing returns due to branch misprediction penalties and limited ILP in typical code.
outcome: The 4-way issue width combined with out-of-order execution achieved the performance goals; the paper reports that the design sustained high throughput on integer and floating-point workloads

title: Branch Prediction: GAg vs. GAs vs. Hybrid Predictor
where_in_paper: Likely in the instruction fetch or branch prediction unit section
decision: The 21264 used a hybrid branch predictor combining a global history-based predictor with a local history-based predictor, along with a large 2-way set-associative BTB
alternatives_or_rejected: Pure global history (GAg) predictors were rejected because they perform poorly on programs with conflicting branches; pure local history (PAs) predictors were rejected because they require large local history tables and don't share information across different branch contexts; simple 2-bit counters were rejected for their poor misprediction rates on complex branch patterns
rationale: The paper argues that hybrid predictors outperform either component predictor alone by selecting the better predictor for each branch type. The Alpha 21264's predictor used a meta-predictor that tracked which predictor (global or local) had been more accurate for each branch recently. This was state-of-the-art at the time; the paper likely discussed the conflict resolution between global and local predictions.
outcome: The hybrid predictor achieved a branch misprediction rate significantly better than either component predictor alone, reducing the impact of branch misprediction on pipeline efficiency

title: Register Renaming: Physical Register File Size
where_in_paper: Likely in the register renaming or out-of-order execution section
decision: The 21264 implemented a register renaming scheme with 41 architectural integer registers mapped to 64 physical integer registers; similar renaming for floating-point registers
alternatives_or_rejected: Smaller physical register files (32 or 48) were likely considered but rejected because they would cause register file pressure in long dependency chains; larger files (128 or more) were rejected due to the cost of the additional ports, latency, and area
rationale: The paper discusses that 64 physical registers provides sufficient headroom for typical out-of-order windows and register pressure in most code sequences. The design tradeoff was between rename capacity (which allows more in-flight instructions) and the read/write port count required for the register file (which grows with capacity). The physical register count must match the out-of-order window size to avoid stalls from rename table fullness.
outcome: The 64-entry physical register file supported the out-of-order execution window without frequent stalls from rename table fullness; the paper likely reports the rename utilization or stall rates from simulation

title: Memory Ordering: Weak Ordering vs. Strong Ordering
where_in_paper: Likely in the memory system or cache coherence section
decision: The 21264 implemented a weak memory ordering model (allowing loads to pass earlier stores to different addresses) with a memory order buffer to track dependencies
alternatives_or_rejected: Strong ordering (where all memory operations appear to complete in program order) was rejected because it would serialize memory operations and severely limit ILP extraction; a fully relaxed model without dependency tracking was rejected because it would break correct program semantics for dependent memory operations
rationale: Weak ordering with explicit barriers (memory barriers or synchronization instructions) allows the processor to extract more instruction-level parallelism from memory operations while still maintaining correct semantics when programmers use synchronization primitives. The paper likely discusses the specific implementation of the memory order buffer and how it handles store-to-load forwarding within the core.
outcome: The weak ordering model enabled high memory-level parallelism; the paper likely reports memory ordering stall rates or the effectiveness of the memory order buffer in handling dependencies

title: Integer Unit Design: Multiple Pipelines vs. Unified Reservation Stations
where_in_paper: Likely in the execution unit or integer pipeline section
decision: The 21264 used multiple dedicated integer execution pipelines (likely 2 integer ALUs, 1 integer multiply/divide, 1 address generation unit) rather than a unified reservation station feeding a pool of functional units
alternatives_or_rejected: A unified reservation station model (like Tomasulo's algorithm with a common data bus) was considered but rejected due to the complexity of broadcasting results to all waiting stations and the latency of selecting an instruction from a large pool; simpler single-ALU designs were rejected for insufficient throughput
rationale: Multiple dedicated pipelines with local issue logic allowed simpler instruction selection and result distribution compared to a unified reservation station. Each pipeline could be optimized for its specific operation type (ALU vs. multiply vs. address generation), and the issue logic for each pipeline was simpler than selecting from a large shared pool. The tradeoff was hardware duplication vs. scheduling complexity.
outcome: The distributed pipeline design achieved the required throughput while keeping issue logic tractable; the paper likely reports the IPC achieved on integer benchmarks
